grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: Ich kann den Stuhl reparieren. · Wir müssen zusammen arbeiten. · Ich will das Heft lesen.

tables.caption: kann ... reparieren · müssen ... arbeiten · will ... lesen

grammar.note_en:
A modal verb adds ability, necessity or intention to another activity. Können means “can / be able to,” müssen “must / have to,” and wollen “want to.” The modal is finite: it changes with its subject and occupies the familiar second position in a statement. The other verb is an infinitive, the basic form naming the activity, at the end: Ich kann den Stuhl reparieren (“I can repair the chair”), Wir müssen zusammen arbeiten (“We have to work together”), Ich will das Heft lesen (“I want to read the notebook”). German uses no extra word corresponding to English “to” after these modals.

The separated finite modal and final infinitive form a bracket around the intervening words. Compare ordinary Ben repariert den Stuhl (“Ben repairs the chair”) with Ben kann den Stuhl reparieren (“Ben can repair the chair”). In these subject-first statements, the object stands between the modal and infinitive. An object can also occupy the first position as a topic; the transformation Den Stuhl will Ben reparieren means “Ben wants to repair the chair.” In a neutral yes/no question the finite modal comes first: Kannst du auch die Tür öffnen? (“Can you open the door too?”), while öffnen stays at the end. With a question word, that word comes first and the finite modal follows it: Was müssen wir machen? (“What do we have to do?”). The story also uses statement-shaped confirmation questions, as in Du kannst reparieren? (“You can repair things?”). The workbook’s arrow items keep the subject word and elicit the verb–subject pair, as in the previous chapter.

The singular forms have no usual -e/-t ending with ich/er: ich kann, er kann; ich muss, er muss; ich will, er will. Du has kannst, musst, willst. Plural wir has können, müssen, wollen; ihr has könnt, müsst, wollt. Each table cell has been demonstrated in the story before its production exercise. The tables limit themselves to the people actually used; no new third-person plural cells are required here. Will is a present wish or intention in German, not the English future auxiliary “will.”

An infinitive often ends in -en: reparieren (“repair”), putzen (“clean”), kochen (“cook”), backen (“bake”), holen (“fetch”), lesen (“read”), sehen (“see”), sitzen (“sit”) and öffnen (“open”). Some surfaces look identical to earlier wir-forms; the modal construction now shows their infinitive job. Sein is the familiar verb “be” in its basic form: Der Laden muss fertig sein (“The shop has to be ready”). Do not add zu before these infinitives. New cards show only forms actually read, including the modal surfaces kann, muss and will.

Keep the meanings distinct. Ich kann nicht reparieren (“I cannot repair things”) gives Mira’s skill limit. Ich will helfen (“I want to help”) gives her intention. Ich muss helfen (“I have to help”) expresses the practical need. Nicht müssen means “not have to / not need to,” not “must not”: Du musst heute nicht backen (“You do not need to bake today”). Nora can bake but there is enough bought bread. The tables and exercises do not introduce a prohibition with müssen. Ada kann heute kommen (“Ada can/may come today”) expresses a possibility; the story does not claim that she has replied.

Ohne means “without” and takes accusative. Ohne Werkzeug (“without tools/equipment”) uses a bare collective noun; ohne den Hammer (“without the hammer”) makes the masculine accusative den visible. Nora brings the picture without the hammer; Lina uses it to hang the picture. Werkzeug can be an individual tool or the collective equipment. Hammer means “hammer,” Nagel “nail,” with plural Nägel. The reference shows actual objects before their use. Arbeit is the work, connected to the familiar arbeiten (“work”).

Kaputt means “broken”; reparieren changes that state. Putzen removes visible dirt, producing sauber (“clean”). Fertig can describe a ready object or a person finished with a task: Der Stuhl ist fertig (“The chair is ready”), Ich bin noch nicht fertig (“I am not finished yet”). Schwer describes a heavy table and difficult work; leicht describes a light chair/hammer and Nora’s easy cleaning task. Nur narrows the focus: nur einen Nagel (“only one nail”), nur hier (“only here”), nicht nur lesen (“not only read”). Selbst emphasizes the actual doer—Ben personally repairs his chair and Mira tests it herself. It need not mean that nobody helps: Mira and Emil contribute to Ben’s repair.

The shared group resolves the immediate worry about paying twice for the same coffee, and contributes different kinds of work. This does not establish lease rights or a permanent charging rule. The final small doors are a cupboard front, still closed; the interior and its contents remain unknown. Its German noun comes in the next chapter.
